newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Ortega set to respect legality of Nicaragua poll.
newsitem.headline: Ortega set to respect legality of Nicaragua poll.

text.p: Left-wing Sandinista leader Daniel Ortega late on Wednesday said his party would recognise the "legality" but not the "legitimacy" of a future government headed by Nicaraguan right-winger Arnoldo Aleman.

After meeting with U.S. ambassador to Nicaragua John Maisto, Ortega said if Nicaraguan electoral officials ratified an Aleman victory in Oct. 20 elections, he would respect the new government's right to exist.

Aleman topped Ortega 51 to 37.7 percent, according to the vote's final tally. But Ortega has refused to concede defeat, demanding new elections be held in two populous departments (provinces) due to alleged irregularities and election fraud.
The Supreme Electoral Council is scheduled to rule on the Sandinista appeal on Nov. 20.
Despite saying that an Aleman government could be legal, Ortega was not entirely conciliatory.

"We are facing a situation of non-legitimacy. Given the high degree of disorganization, disorder and corruption in these elections, we are within our rights to consider them questionable and lacking the consensus of Nicaraguan society," Ortega told reporters.

"The fact that we may face a process that is illegitimate, even though it is legal, doesn't mean we're going to break the constitutional order," he said. "We're going to fight within the legal framework to modify this situation."

Given that world leaders, including U.S. President Bill Clinton and the presidents of all Central American nations but Belize, have recognised Aleman as president elect, there is little chance the election council will overturn his win, political analysts say.

Ortega headed Nicaragua's 1979-1990 left-wing Sandinista government that fought an eight-year war against U.S.-backed Contra rebels. Ortega described his meeting with Maisto as "friendly" and said he felt "very satisfied with the ambassador's efforts in Nicaragua."

Maisto leaves his post in Nicaragua on Friday after more than three years and will head for a probable ambassadorship in Venezuela. He will be replaced by Cuban-American career diplomat Lino Gutierrez, U.S. officials said.
